headline: Gastech opens in Bangkok with 800 speakers and Asian demand as the organising theme
deck: The 54th edition returns to Asia, where the growth in gas demand is, rather than to the places that sell it.
excerpt: Gastech opens at BITEC Bangkok on 14 September for its 54th edition, expecting more than 50,000 professionals and 1,000 exhibitors from over 150 countries, with more than 800 speakers across 200 conference sessions and 18 specialised programmes.
content:
Gastech opens at BITEC in Bangkok on 14 September and runs to the 17th, its 54th edition and its return to Asia. The organisers expect more than 50,000 energy professionals and 1,000 exhibitors from over 150 countries, with more than 800 speakers across 200 conference sessions and 18 specialised programmes.

The event is hosted by Thailand's Ministry of Energy and co-hosted by Chevron, ExxonMobil and Shell. Its declared scope covers natural gas and liquefied natural gas, hydrogen, climate technologies, electrification, digitalisation and artificial intelligence in energy, and shipping and marine.

The choice of host city is the substantive editorial decision behind the week. Gastech has historically alternated between the producing regions and the trading centres. Putting it in Bangkok places it in the middle of the demand growth rather than the supply, and that reflects where the industry's uncertainty currently sits.

The supply side of global LNG is, for the first time in a decade, reasonably well described. Qatar is expanding North Field capacity from 77 million tonnes a year towards 142 million tonnes by 2030. The United States has a large tranche of capacity under construction. The United Arab Emirates is building Ruwais LNG at 9.6 million tonnes a year for commercial operations in 2028. Saudi Arabia has begun producing from Jafurah, the region's largest unconventional gas development, aimed primarily at domestic supply. Broadly, the world knows how much LNG is being built.

What is much less settled is who buys it, on what contract terms, and at what price. Asian demand growth is the swing factor: the pace at which South and Southeast Asian economies substitute gas for coal in power generation, the extent to which price sensitivity in those markets caps volumes, and whether long-term contracts or spot purchasing dominate the next cycle. Sellers with capacity coming online towards the end of this decade need those questions answered before they sign twenty-year offtakes.

That is the conversation a Bangkok edition is designed to host, and it is why the programme is weighted towards commercial structure rather than upstream engineering.

The exhibition floor is organised into four dedicated areas, of which Shipping and Marine is the one that carries most of the physical supply chain content: LNG carriers, marine fuel systems, bunkering, and the terminal and transfer equipment that connects a liquefaction plant to a regasification terminal several thousand miles away.

Gulf participation is substantial at every Gastech, and the region arrives this year with capacity commitments to place rather than volumes to chase. Whether that produces contracts, and on what terms, is the outcome worth watching from Riyadh, Doha and Abu Dhabi.

The exhibition runs at BITEC until 17 September.
author: BrentDesk Staff
scheduledReason: Written before Gastech opens in Bangkok on 14 September. It works from the published programme and independently verified project data, and makes no claim about anything said or announced at the event.
